what_it_does: Silent Data Corruption (SDC) is a rare but serious failure mode in modern processors where a tiny manufacturing defect in an arithmetic circuit causes it to silently produce a wrong answer — no crash, no error message, just subtly incorrect results that can propagate through software undetected. These flaws are increasingly relevant as chip manufacturing becomes more complex and data centers run millions of processors. The paper builds a detailed simulation model (using the gem5 open-source processor simulator) that can inject faults into specific arithmetic units of five real x86 processor designs and measure how often a fault leads to a visible wrong output. The authors then compare the simulation's predictions against real defect rate data collected from large-scale production data centers to estimate how many SDC incidents occur per machine per year across a fleet. The result is, as far as the authors claim, the first public characterization of SDC rates tied to specific processor microarchitectures and instruction types.
